newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian strike causes major disruptions.
newsitem.headline: Colombian strike causes major disruptions.

text.p: A strike by Colombian truck drivers, which entered its second day on Tuesday, has halted all shipments of coffee and other key commodities to the country's ports, exporters said.
"They're not letting anything move out to port, absolutely nothing, we're paralysed," one Bogota-based private coffee exporter said.
"Clients shipping instructions are not going to be fulfilled," she added.

The strike by the Colombian Truck Drivers Association began at midnight Sunday and union spokesmen said it would continue until the government bows to a catalogue of demands, including calls for higher tariffs, lower taxes and tolls and tighter security on highways.
No violence has been reported in connection with the strike, and truckers have mostly refrained from dramatic highway blockades to draw attention to their demands.
But Jorge Ramirez Ocampo, president of the National Exporters Association, said in a telephone interview that all exporters had been adversely affected by the stoppage.

The only truck drivers who have defied a government ban on the blockading of roads were in the northern peninsula of Guajira, where a key road has been barricaded by tractor-trailers since late last week.
Because of the barricades, Colombian coal exports have dropped by 120,000 metric tons since the strike began, industry sources told the Caracol radio network.

Coffee looks set to become the most seriously affected industry, however. Exporters say many shipments will not reach roasters within the promised time of delivery, even if the strike ends by this weekend.
"I see a very big delay in October shipments because of this situation," one bulk coffee exporter told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Even if the strike was settled by Friday, he said, congestion in Colombia's ports threatened to cause worse delays.

Fabio Trujillo, head of the Unidad Cafetera, an independent coffee growers' association in the central city of Manizales, said he had no immediate statistics on how many bags of coffee Colombia had been unable to export so far because of the strike.
But he said truckers had succeeded in sowing "complete chaos" across the country.
"This could have terrible consequences," Trujillo said. "If you can't export, if you can't move coffee around the country internally, then this is a matter of complete chaos," he said.
